rules.name: Ad Hominem (Abusive / Circumstantial)
rules.desc: Attacking an opponent's character, background, appearance, or motives instead of engaging with their substantive argument.

rules.name: Tu Quoque / Whataboutism
rules.desc: Deflecting criticism by accusing the accuser of hypocrisy or raising unrelated counter-allegations.

rules.name: Poisoning the Well
rules.desc: Preemptively presenting adverse information about an opponent to discredit anything they might say beforehand.

rules.name: Genetic Fallacy
rules.desc: Judging the validity of an idea purely on the basis of its origin or source history rather than its merits.

rules.name: Begging the Question (Petitio Principii)
rules.desc: An argument whose premises assume the truth of the conclusion they are supposed to prove.

rules.name: False Dilemma / Forced Dichotomy
rules.desc: Presenting complex, nuanced situations as an either/or choice while ignoring viable middle grounds.

rules.name: Loaded Question
rules.desc: Asking a question containing an unproven, incriminating presumption that cannot be answered simply without admitting guilt.

rules.name: Cherry-Picking (Texas Sharpshooter)
rules.desc: Highlighting only confirming evidence or favorable outliers while ignoring vast contradictory data.

rules.name: Post Hoc Ergo Propter Hoc
rules.desc: Assuming that because Event B occurred after Event A, Event A must have caused Event B.

rules.name: Correlation as Causation
rules.desc: Treating statistical correlation between two variables as definitive proof that one causes the other.

rules.name: Hasty Generalization
rules.desc: Drawing a broad conclusion from a sample that is too small or unrepresentative.

rules.name: Slippery Slope
rules.desc: Claiming that a minor initial step will inevitably trigger a disastrous chain reaction without proving each link.

rules.name: Appeal to Fear (In Terrorem)
rules.desc: Using fabricated, exaggerated, or apocalyptic terror scenarios to coerce acceptance of a claim.

rules.name: Appeal to False Authority
rules.desc: Citing the opinion of a celebrity, non-expert, or authority in an unrelated field as definitive proof.

rules.name: Straw Man Argument
rules.desc: Misrepresenting, exaggerating, or oversimplifying an opponent's argument to make it easier to attack.
